items.title: Microalbuminuria as an early marker
items.contentHtml:
Microalbuminuria as an early marker

  • Microalbuminuria is defined as urinary excretion of albumin between 30 and 300 mg/day or 30-300 mg/g of creatinine in an isolated sample.
  • It is the earliest marker of kidney damage in type 2 diabetes mellitus, preceding the decrease in glomerular filtration.
  • Its detection requires a specific test strip for albumin or albumin/creatinine ratio in a morning urine sample.
  • Annual screening is recommended from diagnosis in type 2 diabetes mellitus and 5 years after diagnosis in type 1 diabetes mellitus.
  • Progression to clinical proteinuria (>300 mg/day) is associated with accelerated loss of kidney function and increased cardiovascular risk.

items.foco: Glomerular filtration rate and KDIGO stages
items.title: Glomerular filtration rate and KDIGO stages
items.contentHtml:
Glomerular filtration rate and KDIGO stages

  • The KDIGO classification stratifies chronic kidney disease according to estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria.
  • eGFR stages: G1 (>90), G2 (60-89), G3a (45-59), G3b (30-44), G4 (15-29) and G5 (<15 ml/min/1.73 m²).
  • The categories of albuminuria are: A1 (<30 mg/g), A2 (30-300 mg/g) and A3 (>300 mg/g).
  • The risk of progression, complications and mortality increases when combining stages. more advanced levels of eGFR and albuminuria.
  • In diabetic nephropathy, the drop in eGFR can occur even without significant albuminuria, especially in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

items.title: Initial glomerular hyperfiltration
items.contentHtml:
Initial glomerular hyperfiltration

  • Glomerular hyperfiltration is defined as an eGFR >125-140 ml/min/1.73 m² in adults, present in the initial stages of diabetes mellitus.
  • Pathophysiology: chronic hyperglycemia → vasodilation of the afferent arteriole and vasoconstriction of the efferent mediated by angiotensin II, increasing intraglomerular pressure.
  • It is an independent predictor of the development of albuminuria and loss of renal function in the long term.
  • The correction of hyperglycemia and the use of inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system can reduce hyperfiltration.
  • Not all patients develop it; Its presence is associated with a higher risk of progression to established diabetic nephropathy.

items.title: Glomerular basement membrane thickening
items.contentHtml:
Glomerular basement membrane thickening

  • It is the earliest histological lesion in diabetic nephropathy, detectable by electron microscopy.
  • It is due to the accumulation of type IV collagen and other extracellular matrix components induced by hyperglycemia.
  • It precedes the appearance of microalbuminuria and can be observed in renal biopsies from diabetic patients without proteinuria.
  • It correlates with the time of evolution of diabetes mellitus and glycemic control.
  • Together with mesangial expansion and glomerular sclerosis, it constitutes the classic histological triad of diabetic nephropathy.

items.foco: Strict blood pressure control with ACEI/ARB2
items.title: Strict blood pressure control with ACEI/ARB2
items.contentHtml:
Strict control of blood pressure with ACEI/ARB

  • The blood pressure goal in diabetic nephropathy is 130/80 mmHg according to current guidelines.
  • First-line drugs are angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) or angiotensin II receptor antagonists (ARA2), due to its antiproteinuric effect independent of lowering blood pressure.
  • It is recommended to start with low doses and titrate to the maximum tolerated dose, monitoring serum creatinine and potassium after 1-2 weeks.
  • An increase in serum creatinine <30% is acceptable; if it is >30%, rule out bilateral renal artery stenosis or hypovolemia.
  • The combination of ACEI and ARB is not recommended due to the increased risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury.

items.title: Target glycated hemoglobin <7%
items.contentHtml:
Glycosylated hemoglobin target <7%

  • The target of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in diabetic nephropathy is <7% to reduce the progression of albuminuria and the deterioration of eGFR.
  • In patients at high risk of hypoglycemia (advanced chronic kidney disease, elderly, polypharmacy), it is individualized with target <8%.
  • Intensive glycemic control (HbA1c <6.5%) has not shown additional benefit and increases the risk of hypoglycemia.
  • HbA1c may be falsely low in advanced renal failure (due to anemia and reduced erythrocyte half-life); fructosamine or continuous glucose monitoring is preferred in these cases.
  • The use of metformin is contraindicated when the eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m² due to the risk of lactic acidosis.

items.foco: Use of SGLT2i and GLP-1 as nephroprotectors
items.title: Use of SGLT2i and GLP-1 as nephroprotectors
items.contentHtml:
Use of SGLT2i and GLP-1 as nephroprotectors

  • Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) reduce the progression of diabetic nephropathy, independently of glycemia, with cardiovascular benefit.
  • Indication: eGFR ≥20 ml/min/1.73 m² in patients with albuminuria A2 or A3; it should be continued until the start of dialysis.
  • The glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor (GLP-1) agonists also show nephroprotection, reducing albuminuria and slowing the fall in eGFR.
  • Both classes reduce intraglomerular pressure and have anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects.
  • Adverse effects of SGLT2i: genital infections, euglycemic ketoacidosis; of GLP-1: nausea, vomiting, risk of pancreatitis.

items.title: Nephrotic syndrome in advanced stages
items.contentHtml:
Nephrotic syndrome in advanced stages

  • The nephrotic syndrome in diabetic nephropathy is characterized by proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia.
  • It typically appears in advanced stages (G3b-G5) with A3 albuminuria, associated with lesions of Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular.
  • Management includes sodium restriction (<2 g/day), loop diuretics (furosemide), and blood pressure control with ACEI or ARB2.
  • Thrombotic risk (renal vein thrombosis) should be evaluated and prophylactic anticoagulation considered if serum albumin <2.5 g/dL.
  • The response to steroids is poor. in diabetic nephropathy; Its presence forces us to rule out another glomerulopathy if there is rapid deterioration.

items.title: Nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions
items.contentHtml:
Nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions

  • Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions are PAS-positive eosinophilic nodules in the glomerular mesangium, pathognomonic of advanced diabetic nephropathy.
  • They represent nodular mesangial sclerosis secondary to accumulation of extracellular matrix, collagen, and deposits of immunoglobulins.
  • They are associated with massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) and rapid progression to end-stage renal failure.
  • In electron microscopy: diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, mesangial expansion and hyaline deposits.
  • Their presence does not require histological confirmation if there is a clinical context of long-standing diabetes mellitus and diabetic retinopathy.

items.title: Association with diabetic retinopathy
items.contentHtml:
Association with diabetic retinopathy

  • Diabetic retinopathy is present in >90% of patients with established diabetic nephropathy, especially in type 1 diabetes mellitus.
  • Both share pathophysiological mechanisms: hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, inflammation and endothelial dysfunction.
  • The absence of retinopathy in a patient with proteinuria should make suspect another nephropathy (non-diabetic glomerulopathy).
  • Proliferative diabetic retinopathy or macular edema are predictors of renal progression.
  • Annual ophthalmological screening is mandatory in all patients with diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy.

items.foco: Hyperkalemia with ACEI in renal failure
items.title: Hyperkalemia with ACEI in renal failure
items.contentHtml:
Hyperkalemia with ACEIs in renal failure

  • ACEIs and ARBs can cause hyperkalemia due to a reduction in aldosterone and a decrease in renal potassium excretion.
  • The risk is greater when eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m², diabetes mellitus, concomitant use of potassium-sparing diuretics, or potassium supplements. Potassium.
  • Serum potassium should be monitored 1-2 weeks after starting or adjusting the dose; if >5.5 mEq/L, temporarily suspend and correct the cause.
  • Management: dietary potassium restriction, use of loop diuretics, and if it persists, consider ion exchange resins (patiromer) or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.
  • Permanently suspending ACEI/ARB is not recommended if hyperkalemia is mild and manageable, due to its benefit. nephroprotective.

items.foco: Indication for biopsy: suspicion of another nephropathy
items.title: Indication for biopsy: suspicion of another nephropathy
items.contentHtml:
Indication for biopsy: suspicion of another nephropathy

  • renal biopsy is indicated in diabetic nephropathy when there is suspicion of another superimposed or alternative nephropathy.
  • Criteria: proteinuria >3.5 g/day without diabetic retinopathy, persistent glomerular hematuria, rapid deterioration of eGFR (>5 ml/min/year), or absence of microalbuminuria in long-standing diabetes mellitus.
  • The most common glomerulopathies to rule out are membranous glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy and focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis.
  • The biopsy is also considered if there is active urinary sediment (casts blood disorders, erythrocyte dysmorphism) or nephrotic syndrome of sudden onset.
  • The risk of bleeding is greater in patients with advanced renal failure; Coagulation evaluation and antiplatelet discontinuation are required.
